name: Facial exercise masks

lead: Facial exercise masks are wearable devices that sit over the face and are meant to work the facial muscles, either through resistance when the wearer makes expressions or through built-in stimulation. They are sold with the aim of firmer, smoother-looking skin and fewer wrinkles.

The idea comes from the wider world of face yoga and facial toning, where practitioners say that building muscle under the skin gives the face a lifted, fuller look. Masks sold under this heading have not been the subject of published studies.

paras: Users wear the mask for short sessions at home, either doing guided expressions against its resistance or letting its stimulation run. Manufacturers' instructions vary by product.

Reported concerns for facial devices in general include skin irritation or pressure marks; stimulation devices carry their own manufacturer warnings. Anyone with skin conditions or implanted devices follows the product's labelled guidance.

web.title: Association of Facial Exercise With the Appearance of Aging
Facial exercises help middle-aged women appear more youthful

angle.text: Makers say working the muscles under the skin gives a lifted, fuller appearance and softens expression lines. The effect is a claimed one based on the facial-exercise concept.

lead: Facial exercise masks are worn over the face to give the muscles resistance or stimulation, with the aim of firmer, fuller-looking cheeks and softer expression lines. Users put one on for short home sessions, either performing expressions against the resistance or letting built-in stimulation run.

The idea extends facial exercise and face yoga, in which people repeat expressions in the hope that stronger facial muscles give a lifted look. A 2018 JAMA Dermatology study of a 20-week home exercise program, without a device, reported fuller upper and lower cheeks and lower estimated age in middle-aged women.[1][2]
Masks as a product type have not been tested in published trials.
infobox: Resistance or stimulation of facial muscles

paras: Products sold as facial exercise masks fall into two broad designs: soft silicone or fabric masks that add resistance to expressions, and masks with built-in electrical or other stimulation. Both aim to engage the muscles of the cheeks, jaw and forehead.

The participants in the 2018 study, women aged 40 to 65, attended two supervised sessions and then practiced a set of facial exercises at home, daily at first and then several times a week for 20 weeks.[1][2] Blinded raters scored standardized photographs and found improvement in upper and lower cheek fullness, and estimated age fell from 50.8 to 48.1 years.[1] Lead author Murad Alam described this as almost a three-year decrease in apparent age.[2] The authors suggested muscle growth under the skin as a possible explanation.[1]
The study was a single-group trial with no control arm; 16 of 27 enrolled participants completed it, and the authors noted the small sample and called for further research.[1]

No studies of facial exercise masks as a product were found. The 2018 JAMA Dermatology research letter, a 20-week single-group trial of device-free facial exercises, reported improved cheek fullness and a lower estimated age, with 16 of 27 participants completing the program.[1]
